label: Person
name: Adalberon of Laon
summary:
Adalberon of Laon (c. 947–1030) was Bishop of Laon and one of the most politically astute and literarily accomplished churchmen of tenth-century France. He is best known for his satirical poem 'Carmen ad Rotbertum Regem' (Song to King Robert), a remarkable document of social and political criticism that expresses profound anxiety about the disorder of his age — the blurring of the three orders of medieval society (oratores, bellatores, laboratores) and what he saw as the dangerous ambitions of the Cluniac monastic reform movement.

Adalberon's poem is one of the earliest explicit formulations of the tripartite theory of medieval society — the division of society into those who pray, those who fight, and those who work — making it a foundational text in the history of medieval social thought. His critique of Cluny reflects the tensions between the old Carolingian ecclesiastical order, in which bishops controlled monasteries, and the new reform monasticism that sought independence from episcopal control.

Politically, Adalberon was a key figure in the transition from the Carolingian to the Capetian dynasty. He played a complex role in the events of 987, when Hugh Capet was elected king of France, and his political manoeuvring contributed to the dynastic transition that shaped France for eight centuries. His bishop of Laon's strategic position between France and the Empire gave him exceptional political leverage.
